Question_text: A jet ski is a type of boat that carries one or two people and travels at high speed on water. Fig. 1.1 shows a student riding on a jet ski. A high-speed jet of water is forced backwards out of the back of the jet ski by a pump inside the jet ski.
image: Fig. 1.1 shows a side view of a person riding a jet ski on water. An arrow indicates 'direction of movement' towards the right. A 'jet of water' is expelled from the back of the jet ski towards the left. Key labels are 'jet ski' and 'jet of water'.

Parts.part_text: The pump increases the momentum of the water that is forced backwards out of the back of the jet ski. Complete the word equation to show the relationship between the resultant force on an object and the change in momentum of the object. resultant force =
In 2.0s, the pump increases the backwards speed of 180 kg of water by 30m/s. Calculate the backwards force exerted on the water.
Using Newton's third law of motion, explain why there is a forwards force on the jet ski.
The student has a mass of 70kg and the jet ski has a mass of 280 kg. Use your answer from (a)(ii) to determine the acceleration of the student and jet ski when no resistive forces are acting.
The jet ski reaches a speed of 20 m/s. Calculate the total kinetic energy of the student and jet ski at this speed.

Question_text: A glass beaker of mass m is at rest on a horizontal surface. The base of the beaker is a circle with a radius r.

Parts.part_text: The beaker exerts a pressure on the horizontal surface. Determine an expression for the pressure in terms of the gravitational field strength g, m and r.

Fig. 2.1 shows the beaker being filled with a liquid from container X. Initially, the beaker is empty. At time t = 0, the tap is opened and liquid from container X flows slowly into the beaker at a constant rate. At time t = T, the liquid stops flowing into the beaker. Sketch on Fig. 2.2 to show how the pressure exerted on the horizontal surface varies between t = 0 and t = 2T.

Labels include 'beaker', 'tap', 'container X', and 'horizontal surface'. Fig. 2.2 is a blank graph with y-axis 'pressure' and x-axis 't'. The x-axis is marked with 0, T, and 2T. Question_text: Fig. 3.1 shows a laboratory freezer. The door is closed and the freezer is switched on. A cold liquid is pumped through the copper pipe at the top of the freezer. The temperature of the air next to the copper pipe decreases quickly.
image: Fig. 3.1 shows a cutaway diagram of a laboratory freezer. A 'copper pipe' is located at the top inside. The walls of the freezer are thick and labeled 'thick insulation'.

Parts.part_text: Explain how the temperature of the rest of the air in the freezer decreases.

The thick insulation shown in Fig. 3.1 is made from a plastic material. The plastic material in the insulation is a poor thermal conductor. Describe how thermal energy is transferred through a plastic material.
The plastic material also contains a large number of small air bubbles. Explain how the air bubbles reduce the transfer of thermal energy through the insulation.

Question_text: Fig. 4.1 shows a large syringe that is sealed at the nozzle by wax. There is a piston inside the syringe. The pressure of the air inside the syringe is equal to atmospheric pressure, 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa. The volume of the air inside the syringe is 1.2 × 10⁻⁴ m³. The area of the end of the piston that is in contact with the air is 3.5 × 10⁻³ m². The friction between the piston and the syringe is negligible.
image: Fig. 4.1 shows a cross-section of a syringe. The left end is sealed by 'wax' in the 'nozzle'. A 'piston' is inside, with its 'face of piston' interacting with 'air' inside the syringe. Labels include 'syringe', 'nozzle', 'wax', 'air', 'face of piston', 'piston'.

Parts.part_text: Calculate the force on the piston due to the pressure of the air inside the syringe.
The force on the piston in (a)(i) acts to the right. Explain why the piston does not move to the right.

The piston is now pulled to the right by an additional force. The temperature of the air in the syringe does not change. Explain, in terms of particles, why the pressure of the air in the syringe decreases.
Calculate the pressure of the air inside the syringe when the volume of the air is 1.5 x 10⁻⁴ m³.

Question_text: Fig. 6.1 shows the circuit symbol for a relay and two labelled terminals. The heater transfers energy at a rate of 40W when it is connected to a 12V supply.

Calculate: the resistance of the heater.

Question_text: The isotope thorium-230 (²³⁰Th) decays by alpha particle (α-particle) emission.

Parts.part_text: Describe the composition of an α-particle.
State the name of the particle that is identical in composition to an α-particle.
The α-particle decay of thorium-230 produces an isotope of radium. Deduce: the number of neutrons in a neutral atom of this isotope of radium
Deduce: the number of electrons in a neutral atom of this isotope of radium.
The half-life of thorium-230 is 75000 years. A radioactive sample contains 7.2 × 10¹⁶ thorium-230 atoms. Determine the time it takes for the number of thorium-230 atoms to decrease to 9.0 × 10¹⁵.

When it decays, thorium-230 also emits gamma radiation (γ-radiation). Fig. 8.1 shows a narrow beam of γ-radiation passing into an electric field. On Fig. 8.1, sketch the path of the γ-radiation in the electric field.

Question_text: The Earth has a radius of 6.4 × 10⁶ m and rotates on its axis once in every 24 hours.

Parts.part_text: Explain why the speed around the axis of rotation of an object on the Earth decreases as the distance of the object from the equator increases.
The Earth moves around the Sun because a force acts on the Earth. State what provides this force.
The orbit of the Earth around the Sun is an ellipse. Describe what happens to the magnitude of the force that acts on the Earth as it moves in this elliptical orbit.
Explain why the Earth travels the slowest when it is at its furthest distance from the Sun.
